transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
President Trump has announced that Stephen Miller will take over as the new White House
chief of staff.
Miller, who is currently the deputy chief of staff, will replace Suzy Wiles starting
on Monday.
NPR's Danielle Kurt Slaben reports the shake up follows Republican midterm losses that
handed Democrats control of the House and Senate.
>> President Trump announced the personnel change on social media saying Miller will
take over the position on Monday, November 9th.
Wiles worked with the Trump 2020 campaign in Florida and has served as chief of staff
in this White House from day one of this administration.
She's the first woman to hold the position.
In his social media post, Trump says she will be moving to the Trump political operation.
Miller has been a fixture in Trump's circle since 2016 and is considered one of the president's
most trusted and aggressive advisers.
He is known in particular for being an architect of the president's anti-immigration policies.
Danielle Kurt Slaben, NPR News, the White House.
>> Pope Leo is in Uruguay, the first stop on his three-country 12-day visit to Latin
America.
Just weeks since his lung cancer surgery, the 71-year-old Pope gave a long welcome address
and held evening prayers in Montevideo's main cathedral, NPR's Kari Khan reports.
>> The crowds have been small but enthusiastic for Leo, the first papal visit in nearly four
decades to Latin America's most secular nation.
Leo didn't wait long to urge more religiosity in public life and criticize Uruguay's pioneering
law legalizing abortion.
Whoever has not yet been born already belongs to the human family and to the future, he
said, deserving all dignity and protection.
Only about a third of Uruguayans identify as Catholic.
Leo addressed Uruguay's public secularism with the president at his side.
He urged that religion not be confined just to the private sphere.
Kari Khan, NPR News, Montevideo.
>> Mr. Chris Murphy has been released from the hospital less than a week after having
a stroke.
The Connecticut Democrat is heading to rehab as Molly Ingram of member station WSHU reports.
>> In his first statement since suffering a stroke last Saturday, Murphy says he was
diagnosed with a small bleed in the thalamus region of his brain.
The 53-year-old said he felt numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game and decided
to call 911.
Murphy said the experience has been scary for him and his family and thanked doctors
and staff at the Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore.
According to his office, Murphy will spend the next several weeks in rehab and will miss
votes while he recovers.
His doctor said in a statement that Murphy was making tremendous progress and is expected
to make a full recovery.
For NPR News, I'm Molly Ingram in Fairfield, Connecticut.
>> This is NPR News.
Researchers in Massachusetts have narrowly rejected a ballot measure aimed at boosting
the supply of starter homes.
NPR's Jennifer Ludden reports the change would have overridden local zoning rules.
>> The measure would have allowed single-family homes to be built on small lots of 5,000 square
feet.
Most residential land in the state currently requires an acre or more per home.
Supporters of the ballot measure said large lots mean fewer homes get built and those
that do are bigger and more expensive.
A growing number of states, blue and red, have changed zoning to allow smaller homes
on smaller lots, and the Massachusetts measure had brought support from elected officials
and business groups.
But critics opposed the loss of local control, and they argued that smaller lots in greater
density would not guarantee that the new homes built would actually be affordable.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News.
>> The Trump administration is moving ahead with plans for a massive memorial arch, even
as a federal court temporarily blocks construction.
A website launched on Friday showcases the proposed 250-foot structure located between
the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.
Plans include space for events, munitions storage, and positions for snipers.
Trump's construction and renovation projects could face greater scrutiny when Democrats
take control of Congress in January, but for now, construction remains on hold under a
court order.
I'm Windsor Johnston, NPR News, in Washington.

Pope Leo begins 12-day Latin America trip in Uruguay, urging religion's public role
